start.text:
CASE BRIEF
Daniel Okafor, 34M — Secondary school teacher


TRIAGE VITALS
HR 104 | BP 118/76 | RR 22 | Temp 38.9°C | SpO₂ 94% | Pain 4/10


HISTORY
Presenting complaint: Fever and worsening cough × 3 days. 'I thought it was just a cold, but I'm not getting better.'

Respiratory: Productive cough — initially dry, now yellow-green sputum. Sharp right-sided chest pain worse with breathing and coughing (pleuritic). Progressive dyspnoea — winded walking to the bathroom. No haemoptysis. No wheeze.

Systemic: Fever onset 72 h ago. One episode of rigors night 1. Sweats, myalgia, fatigue — off work yesterday. No recent travel. No known sick contacts. Poor oral intake × 2 days.

Urinary: No dysuria, frequency, haematuria, or loin pain.

PMHx / Background:
• Mild intermittent asthma — last used salbutamol 3 months ago
• NKDA | Medications: salbutamol PRN
• Smoker — 10 cigarettes/day × 12 years (~6 pack-years)
• Lives alone. No flu vaccination this year.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
EXAMINATION
General: Alert, flushed, mildly distressed; splinting on the right.
Hands/neck: No clubbing, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy.

Chest:
• Reduced expansion right side
• Percussion: dull right lower zone
• Auscultation: bronchial breath sounds + increased vocal resonance + fine inspiratory crackles at right base; reduced air entry right lower lobe
• No wheeze

Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No rash, no oedema.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
CLINICAL IMPRESSION
Right lower zone signs consistent with lobar consolidation. Combined with pleuritic chest pain, purulent sputum, rigors, and fever × 3 days in a smoker — community-acquired pneumonia is the leading diagnosis.

SpO₂ 94% requires immediate supplemental oxygen. Confirm with CXR, draw bloods and blood cultures before antibiotics, assess severity with CURB-65, administer antibiotics early, and decide on disposition.

history-respiratory.text:
Daniel's respiratory history:

• Productive cough for 3 days — initially dry, now producing yellow-green sputum
• Right-sided sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing and coughing (pleuritic)
• Progressively worsening breathlessness — he's been winded walking to the bathroom
• No haemoptysis
• No wheeze (his asthma has been well-controlled for years)

This history is strongly suggestive of a lower respiratory tract infection — the pleuritic component and productive purulent sputum raise concern for pneumonia over viral bronchitis.

history-systemic.text:
Systemic history:

• Fever started 72 hours ago — initially 37.8°C, now 38.9°C at triage
• One episode of rigors on night 1
• Moderate sweats, particularly at night
• Significant myalgia and fatigue — he could not go to work yesterday
• No recent travel (never left the country)
• No sick contacts that he is aware of
• Loss of appetite, very poor oral intake over 2 days

No rash, no neck stiffness, no headache — making meningitis less likely. The fever duration and rigors are more characteristic of bacterial than purely viral illness.

investigation-hub.text:
You have enough clinical information to direct your investigation.

Current working differential:
1. Community-acquired pneumonia (most likely)
2. Viral LRTI / bronchitis (possible but less likely given purulent sputum, rigors, exam)
3. Urinary source (very unlikely — no urinary symptoms)

What investigations do you want to order?
investigation-hub.hint: For suspected pneumonia, three investigations are critical: a Chest X-ray (to visualise the lungs), blood tests including CBC, CRP and blood cultures (to confirm infection and identify the organism), and blood cultures MUST be drawn before any antibiotics are given or they become useless. Order the CXR and bloods first.

15 minutes later — Laboratory

BLOOD RESULTS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CBC:
  WBC: 14.8 ×10⁹/L ↑ (ref 4–11) — Neutrophilia: 12.1 ×10⁹/L ↑
  Haemoglobin: 143 g/L (normal)

severity-assessment.text:
CURB-65 SEVERITY ASSESSMENT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
C — Confusion (new): No → 0
U — Urea >7 mmol/L: Borderline (creatinine mildly elevated, urea not checked) → 0
R — Respiratory rate ≥30/min: No (RR 22) → 0
B — BP systolic <90 or diastolic <60: No → 0
6 — Age ≥65: No → 0

CURB-65 score: 0

Score 0–1: Mild CAP — consider home treatment
Score 2: Moderate CAP — consider admission
Score ≥3: Severe CAP — hospital admission, ICU consideration

─────────────────────────────────────────────────
However — CURB-65 alone does not tell the full story:
• SpO₂ 94% on air — clinically significant hypoxaemia
• PCT 2.8, WBC 14.8, CRP 142 — significant systemic response
• Moderate dehydration
• Lives alone — poor social support if deteriorates
• Pre-existing asthma

Clinical judgment here is essential. A CURB-65 of 0 with SpO₂ 94% and these inflammatory markers warrants admission for IV antibiotics and monitoring — the score alone underestimates severity in this case.

treatment-decision.text:
Daniel is sitting in the acute bay. SpO₂ 95% on 2L O₂ via nasal prongs. He is comfortable enough to answer questions. RR 22.

You have confirmed:
• Right lower lobe pneumonia on CXR
• Significant inflammatory response (WBC 14.8, CRP 142, PCT 2.8)
• SpO₂ 94% on air → 95% on supplemental oxygen
• Mild renal impairment likely from dehydration

What is your treatment plan?
treatment-decision.hint: His low SpO₂ and abnormal inflammatory markers mean he cannot be safely discharged — CURB-65 = 0 does not override clinical judgement. He needs hospital admission, IV antibiotics covering both typical and atypical bacteria (dual therapy), and IV fluids for dehydration. Ensure blood cultures were drawn BEFORE starting antibiotics.

ward-deterioration.text:
30 minutes later — Ward Nurse Alert

The ward nurse pages you urgently. Daniel's observations:

HR 118 | BP 98/60 | RR 26 | SpO₂ 89% on 2L O₂ | Temp 39.6°C

He is increasingly confused and cannot tell you today's date. He now meets Sepsis-3 criteria — new organ dysfunction has developed since admission.

The ward team have no management plan to act on. There are no standing antibiotic orders, no fluid plan, no escalation criteria documented.

effects.reason: Patient admitted to ward without antibiotics, diagnosis, or management plan — deteriorated to sepsis

ward-admitted-no-treatment.text:
Daniel deteriorates to sepsis on the ward.

Within 30 minutes of admission, his observations collapse. The ward team have no management plan to act on — no standing antibiotic orders, no fluid prescription, no escalation criteria documented. They escalate to the medical registrar, who transfers him to the High Dependency Unit.

HDU course: IV antibiotics commenced, vasopressors required overnight, non-invasive ventilation for 18 hours. Stepped down day 4, discharged day 9.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

You admitted Daniel to the ward before establishing treatment.

Admission is a disposition decision — it determines where the patient goes, not what happens to them. The ward is a monitoring environment, not a resuscitation space. Without IV antibiotics, IV fluids, and a documented management plan already in motion at the time of admission:
• The ward team received an acutely unwell, untreated patient
• There were no standing orders to guide escalation
• When Daniel deteriorated, there was nothing in place to fall back on

The correct sequence for moderate-severe CAP:
  ✗  Admit → then treat (too late — patient deteriorates in transit)
  ✓  Diagnose → treat (IV antibiotics + O₂ + fluids in ED) → then admit with a plan

Door-to-antibiotic time is measured from diagnosis, not from ward arrival. Starting antibiotics in the ED before admission is a measurable quality standard — and the standard you missed here.

One hour later — URGENT

The nurse calls you urgently. Daniel has deteriorated:

HR 122 | BP 96/58 | RR 28 | SpO₂ 88% on 2L O₂ | Temp 39.8°C

He is now confused — he cannot tell you the correct date.

He meets Sepsis-3 criteria:
• Suspected infection ✓
• Acute organ dysfunction: SOFA score increased ≥2
  — New confusion (CNS)
  — SpO₂ 88% despite supplemental O₂ (respiratory)
  — BP 96/58 (cardiovascular)

This patient is in SEPSIS. The delay in antibiotics has allowed systemic progression. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.

You must act immediately.

choices.text: Sepsis bundle: blood cultures NOW, IV antibiotics, IV fluid bolus, high-flow O₂, urgent bloods, escalate

inappropriate-discharge.text:
Daniel is discharged with: oral amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days and advice to return if he worsens.

He deteriorates at home overnight. His partner calls an ambulance at 03:00.

On arrival: HR 128 | BP 88/52 | RR 32 | SpO₂ 82% on air | Temp 40.1°C

He is admitted to the ICU with septic shock requiring non-invasive ventilation and vasopressors.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

CURB-65 = 0 does not always mean safe to discharge. Clinical context always overrides scoring tools:
• SpO₂ 94% on air is clinically significant and requires O₂ — this alone warrants admission for monitoring
• PCT 2.8 ng/mL indicates significant systemic bacterial response
• Mild renal impairment from dehydration requires IV fluids
• Lives alone — poor social support

Oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up are appropriate for mild CAP (CURB-65 0–1, no hypoxaemia, no comorbidities). This case did not meet that threshold.

Nursing staff realise blood cultures were never drawn before the antibiotics started. They ask if you want them drawn now.

Note: Once antibiotics are in the bloodstream, blood cultures have significantly reduced yield. The opportunity to identify the causative organism has likely passed.

What do you do next?

sepsis-rescue.text:
The sepsis bundle is initiated promptly once you recognise the deterioration:
• Blood cultures ×2 drawn
• IV piperacillin-tazobactam commenced (broader spectrum given sepsis)
• IV doxycycline added for atypical cover
• 500 mL IV crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes
• High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
• Urgent repeat bloods including lactate (2.8 mmol/L — elevated)

Daniel is transferred to the High Dependency Unit (HDU) for monitoring.

Over the next 24 hours he improves: fevers resolve, SpO₂ stabilises on 4L O₂, blood pressure normalises. He is stepped down to the ward on day 2 and discharged on day 5.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Withholding antibiotics to await culture results is not justified in a patient with confirmed pneumonia, hypoxaemia, and elevated PCT. This approach caused preventable deterioration to sepsis. While the outcome was ultimately good, the delay added patient risk, ICU resource utilisation, and a longer hospital stay.

Key teaching: In moderate-to-severe CAP, antibiotics should be administered within 1 hour of diagnosis. Culture results inform de-escalation — not the initial decision.

outcome-excellent.text:
Daniel Okafor is admitted to the respiratory medicine ward under the general medicine team.

Treatment summary:
• IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g q8h
• Oral doxycycline 100mg BD
• IV normal saline 1L over 4 hours (for rehydration)
• Supplemental O₂ via nasal prongs, titrated ≥94%
• Paracetamol 1g q6h (antipyretic and analgesia)
• Thromboprophylaxis: low-molecular-weight heparin per protocol

Clinical course:
Day 1: Fevers reduce, feels slightly better
Day 2: Oral intake improving, SpO₂ 96% on air
Day 3: Apyrexial, SpO₂ 97% on room air, switched to oral antibiotics
Day 4: Discharged home with 5 days of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and doxycycline

Blood cultures: No growth after 5 days — common in CAP (organism identified in only ~25% of hospitalised CAP cases).

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Excellent work. This was a textbook approach to moderate community-acquired pneumonia:

✓ Early oxygen for SpO₂ 94%
✓ CXR confirming right lower lobe consolidation
✓ Blood cultures before antibiotics (antibiotic stewardship)
✓ Dual-agent therapy (beta-lactam + atypical cover)
✓ IV route for moderate severity + hypoxaemia
✓ IV fluids for mild pre-renal impairment
✓ Admission decision with clinical judgment beyond CURB-65

outcome-excellent-with-sputum.text:
Daniel is admitted to the respiratory medicine ward.

Sputum gram stain: Gram-positive diplococci — consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Sputum culture (day 2): S. pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin — de-escalation to IV amoxicillin alone on day 2.

Treatment course:
Day 1–2: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate + doxycycline
Day 2 onwards: IV amoxicillin (de-escalated based on sensitivities)
Day 4: Switched to oral amoxicillin and discharged

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Exceptional performance. Your sputum culture enabled antibiotic de-escalation — a hallmark of good antibiotic stewardship. This reduces adverse effects, Clostridioides difficile risk, and selection pressure for resistant organisms.

A small but meaningful clinical win that reflects the habits of an excellent clinician.

cbc.text: CBC back. WBC is elevated with a neutrophilia — consistent with an acute bacterial process. Haemoglobin is normal, platelets are normal. The picture points to a focal bacterial infection, not a systemic or haematological cause.

cbc.reason: Blood tests drawn (CBC) — essential workup for suspected bacterial infection

bmp.text: BMP back. Electrolytes are fine — sodium and potassium both normal. Creatinine is mildly elevated at 104 µmol/L, consistent with pre-renal impairment from two days of poor oral intake and reduced fluid intake. Not severe, but clinically relevant: IV fluids are appropriate to address dehydration, and NSAIDs should be avoided given the renal context. Urea is not part of this panel — check it separately if you need a precise CURB-65 score.

crp.text: CRP is markedly elevated — this level of inflammation is consistent with a significant bacterial infection. Combined with the CXR findings and clinical picture, it reinforces the diagnosis of CAP and the need for prompt antibiotic treatment.

blood-cultures.text: Blood cultures collected and sent to microbiology. Results will take 24–48 hours. If a bacteraemia is present and cultures were drawn before antibiotics, there is a good chance of isolating the organism — potentially allowing de-escalation of therapy based on sensitivities.

Blood cultures collected and sent — however, antibiotics were administered before collection. The yield of blood cultures taken after antibiotics is significantly reduced. In future, always draw cultures first.

blood-cultures.reason: Blood cultures collected before antibiotics — correct practice preserving microbiological data

procalcitonin.text: Procalcitonin is elevated, supporting a bacterial rather than viral aetiology. While it is primarily useful for guiding antibiotic duration and de-escalation decisions, it adds weight to the diagnosis of bacterial CAP.

lactate.text: Lactate is within normal limits. This is reassuring — a significantly elevated lactate would raise concern for septic shock and trigger a more aggressive resuscitation approach. For now, Daniel does not meet septic shock criteria.

abg.text: ABG (room air): pH 7.42, PaO₂ 68 mmHg, PaCO₂ 36 mmHg, HCO₃ 23 mmol/L — Type 1 (hypoxaemic) respiratory failure. PaO₂ 68 mmHg confirms significant hypoxaemia. The low PaCO₂ reflects compensatory tachypnoea; Daniel is not tiring and there is no CO₂ retention. Normal bicarbonate confirms this is acute, not chronic. Importantly, this rules out Type 2 failure which would demand a more cautious oxygen delivery strategy. Continue supplemental oxygen targeting SpO₂ ≥ 94%.

urinalysis.text: Urinalysis: clear, leukocyte esterase negative, nitrites negative, WBC 0–2/hpf — within normal limits. A urinary source has been effectively excluded. While it is always appropriate to consider urinary sepsis in a febrile patient, Daniel has no urinary symptoms whatsoever and his clinical picture is entirely respiratory. This test adds 20 minutes without changing your management — the higher-priority workup (CXR, bloods) should take precedence.

This further supports a bacterial aetiology. Combined with the elevated inflammatory markers and right lower lobe consolidation on CXR, community-acquired pneumonia caused by a bacterial organism is now your working diagnosis. Preliminary gram stain (available within hours): gram-positive diplococci — consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common CAP pathogen. oxygen.text: You apply supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs, targeting SpO₂ ≥ 95%. Daniel's laboured breathing eases slightly within a few minutes. Keeping his saturations up is the priority while you work through the workup.

oxygen.reason: Supplemental oxygen applied for SpO₂ < 95% — correct first step

amoxicillin-clavulanate-iv.text: You prescribe amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV — a broad-spectrum beta-lactam covering the most common CAP pathogens including Streptococcus pneumoniae. The nurse confirms the dose is running. This marks your door-to-antibiotic time — an important quality metric for hospitalised CAP. Earlier is better.

amoxicillin-clavulanate-iv.reason: Appropriate beta-lactam antibiotic (amoxicillin-clavulanate IV) administered — core CAP treatment

Two beta-lactam antibiotics prescribed — amoxicillin-clavulanate and ceftriaxone have overlapping cover. Dual beta-lactam therapy adds toxicity without benefit; dual-agent CAP therapy means a beta-lactam plus an atypical agent (e.g. doxycycline), not two beta-lactams.

doxycycline-po.text: Doxycycline 100 mg PO added to cover atypical organisms — Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila, and Legionella. In a 34-year-old community case, atypical pathogens account for a significant proportion of CAP and should not be overlooked. Dual-agent coverage is standard.

normal-saline-bolus.text: 500 mL normal saline bolus commenced. Daniel has had poor oral intake for two days and his tachycardia likely has a dehydration component alongside the infection. A fluid challenge is appropriate, and the mildly elevated creatinine supports giving IV fluids to protect renal function.

normal-saline-bolus.reason: IV fluids given for tachycardia and dehydration

acetaminophen-iv.text: Paracetamol 1 g IV administered. Within 30 minutes Daniel's pleuritic chest pain eases noticeably and his temperature begins to trend down. Regular paracetamol is first-line analgesia for pleuritic pain — it is safe with his mildly elevated creatinine (unlike NSAIDs), has a reliable antipyretic effect, and improves patient comfort while you work through the definitive workup.

ceftriaxone.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV commenced — a third-generation cephalosporin with good activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and other typical CAP pathogens. However, ceftriaxone has no activity against atypical organisms: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila are all intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams. IDSA/ATS CAP guidelines recommend dual-agent therapy for hospitalised patients — a beta-lactam plus an atypical agent (e.g. doxycycline or azithromycin). Consider adding doxycycline to complete your regimen.

ceftriaxone.reason: Antibiotic (ceftriaxone) administered — appropriate beta-lactam for CAP; note: add atypical cover (doxycycline) to complete dual-agent therapy

Two beta-lactam antibiotics prescribed — amoxicillin-clavulanate and ceftriaxone have overlapping cover. Dual beta-lactam therapy adds toxicity without benefit; dual-agent CAP therapy means a beta-lactam plus an atypical agent (e.g. doxycycline), not two beta-lactams.

ibuprofen.text: Ibuprofen 400 mg PO administered for pleuritic pain and fever. NSAIDs are effective analgesics and have an antipyretic effect — pleuritic pain often responds well to them. However, Daniel has mild creatinine elevation consistent with dehydration. NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis and can worsen pre-renal acute kidney injury. Paracetamol is the safer first-line choice here. If NSAIDs are continued, monitor renal function closely and ensure adequate fluid resuscitation.

ibuprofen.reason: NSAIDs prescribed to a patient with pre-renal creatinine elevation — NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandins and can precipitate acute kidney injury. Paracetamol is the correct first-line analgesic here.

draw-blood-cultures.text: You draw two sets of blood cultures — one from each arm — using full sterile technique and send them to microbiology. Results take 24–48 hours. If a bacteraemia is present and cultures were drawn before antibiotics, there is a good chance of isolating the organism, enabling targeted de-escalation of therapy.

Blood cultures drawn and sent to microbiology — however, antibiotics were already administered before collection. The yield of cultures taken after antibiotic exposure is significantly reduced. In future, always draw cultures before giving antibiotics to preserve microbiological data.

draw-blood-cultures.reason: Blood cultures collected before antibiotics — correct practice preserving microbiological data

severity-assessment.text: You apply the CURB-65 score. Confusion — no (0). Urea not yet available — assume 0. Respiratory rate ≥ 30 — RR is 22, so 0. Blood pressure < 90/60 — BP is 118/76, so 0. Age ≥ 65 — Daniel is 34, so 0. CURB-65 = 0. By guideline, a score of 0 suggests potential outpatient management — but CURB-65 is a tool, not a decision. Daniel has SpO₂ 94% on air, significant systemic inflammatory markers, mild pre-renal impairment, and lives alone. Clinical judgement overrides the score: he requires hospital admission for IV antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and monitoring.

severity-assessment.reason: CAP severity assessed using CURB-65 — guides antibiotic route and disposition decision

admit-to-ward.text: You admit Daniel to the respiratory medicine ward. The bed manager is notified and a bed allocated. Nursing staff complete the admission assessment and attach him to continuous monitoring. A ward plan will need to be documented once investigations and treatment are underway.

admit-to-ward.reason: Patient admitted to ward — correct disposition for moderate CAP with hypoxaemia

iv-access-peripheral.text: 18G peripheral IV cannula sited in the right antecubital fossa, flushed and confirmed patent. Good preparation — IV access is needed before any IV medications or fluids can be given. The nursing staff note the cannula in Daniel's chart.

12-lead-ecg-monitoring.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring applied. In any acutely unwell patient with tachycardia, baseline ECG monitoring is appropriate standard care — it catches arrhythmias and rate changes early. The monitor shows sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm; no arrhythmia, no ST changes. The tachycardia is consistent with the fever, pain, and systemic infection. No cardiac concern at this time.
